results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, with at least two supportive criteria (clear levodopa response, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor of a limb, olfactory loss) and no absolute exclusion criteria. Clear levodopa response is a major supportive criterion.

results.authors: Tolosa E, Wenning G, Poewe W
results.key_finding: Wearing-off (end-of-dose deterioration) occurs in up to 50% of PD patients within 5 years of initiating levodopa therapy. Management strategies include fractionating levodopa doses, adding catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors (entacapone), adding MAO-B inhibitors, or introducing dopamine agonists. Predictable wearing-off differs from random motor fluctuations.

results.key_finding: DaTscan (I-123 ioflupane SPECT) identifies presynaptic dopaminergic deficit with high sensitivity and specificity for neurodegenerative parkinsonism. prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, promethazine, or other phenothiazine/butyrophenone antiemetics in a patient with Parkinson's disease

required_recommendations: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: confirm clinically established PD with bradykinesia plus resting tremor and rigidity, prior clear levodopa response (supportive criterion), and absence of absolute exclusion criteria

Recognize prochlorperazine as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (phenothiazine class) that is contraindicated in PD and can worsen motor symptoms even with intermittent use; substitute ondansetron for migraine-associated nausea

Identify elevated TSH (5.8 mIU/L) indicating suboptimal levothyroxine replacement; adjust levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 6 weeks, as hypothyroidism can independently worsen fatigue and motor slowing
Characterize motor fluctuations as predictable end-of-dose wearing-off based on symptom diary and initiate appropriate management (fractionated dosing, COMT inhibitor, or MAO-B inhibitor)
Verify correct timing of levothyroxine (empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before carbidopa-levodopa) to prevent absorption interference
Document pre-motor features (anosmia, constipation) predating PD diagnosis by 5-7 years as supportive of idiopathic synucleinopathy rather than drug-induced parkinsonism
Assess fall risk formally and refer to physical therapy for gait and balance training including freezing-of-gait strategies

key_clinical_evidence: Predictable end-of-dose wearing-off emerging 4 years after PD diagnosis is a classic pharmacokinetic complication of levodopa therapy, not a sign of misdiagnosis

Prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine dopamine D2 antagonist) used intermittently for migraine nausea is contraindicated in PD and can significantly worsen motor symptoms; it is the primary actionable drug red herring

Elevated TSH (5.8 mIU/L) is an important actionable finding; suboptimal thyroid replacement is an independent reversible contributor to fatigue and motor slowing but does not explain the tremor, asymmetry, or levodopa responsiveness

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis under the MDS criteria; laboratory testing excludes a mimic when one is suspected.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Rosa Elena Vega is a 58-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with a 4-year history of Parkinson's disease who presents to the movement disorders clinic accompanied by her husband for evaluation of worsening motor fluctuations and increasingly frequent freezing of gait. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 54 following a 12- to 18-month history of progressive left hand rest tremor, left arm stiffness, and generalized slowing. At diagnosis she had an excellent response to levodopa with greater than 50% improvement in motor scores and was titrated to her current regimen of carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg four times daily. For approximately the first two years she had excellent motor control throughout the day. However, over the past 18 months she has noticed that the benefit from each levodopa dose seems to wear off approximately 2.5 hours after ingestion. She keeps a symptom diary and consistently notes return of left-hand tremor, bilateral stiffness, bradykinesia, and freezing episodes during these predictable OFF windows. The OFF periods last approximately 30 to 45 minutes until the next dose takes effect. She reports four distinct OFF periods per day, each associated with subjective stiffness, slowing, difficulty initiating movement, and two to three freezing-of-gait episodes per week. She has had two actual falls in the past three months, occurring when she froze while walking through doorways. She denies any involuntary writhing movements (dyskinesias) at peak dose. Her husband reports that during OFF periods she is visibly more rigid and speaks more softly, and that her facial expression becomes even more mask-like. She denies any visual hallucinations, significant cognitive complaints beyond occasional word-finding difficulty, or urinary incontinence. She reports long-standing constipation predating her PD diagnosis by approximately five years, managed with fiber supplementation. She also notes hyposmia for at least six to seven years, which she initially attributed to chronic allergies. She has a history of chronic migraine and uses sumatriptan for acute attacks. Approximately twice per month she requires prochlorperazine 10 mg for severe nausea accompanying migraines, a practice that predates her PD diagnosis by several years. Her husband and her neurologist are concerned that the prochlorperazine use could be contributing to worsening Parkinsonian symptoms. Her hypothyroidism was diagnosed three years ago and she is currently taking levothyroxine 75 mcg daily; her most recent TSH was measured six months ago. She denies new medications, recent infections, or other intercurrent illnesses. A maternal history of Parkinson's disease has made her particularly anxious about disease progression.

neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (fails to habituate after 10 taps). Seborrheic dermatitis on scalp and nasolabial folds. Micrographia demonstrated on writing sample — letters progressively smaller and trailing off. No myoclonus. End-of-dose symptom diary reviewed: patient documents return of stiffness, tremor, and freezing approximately 2.5 hours after each levodopa dose, lasting 30-45 minutes prior to next dose ('OFF' periods 4 times daily).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact bilaterally. Dysdiadochokinesia left hand attributable to bradykinesia. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements full in all directions without nystagmus or supranuclear gaze palsy. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. Facial expression markedly hypomimic with reduced spontaneous blink rate (approximately 5 blinks per minute). Mild dysarthria without hypernasality. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Reduced stride length bilaterally with marked reduction of left arm swing; right arm swing mildly reduced. Stooped posture. En bloc turning (requires 5-6 steps to turn 180 degrees). Freezing of gait observed on initiation from standstill and when passing through doorway. Start-hesitation present. Tandem walking impaired. Pull test: two retropulsive steps before recovery. Falls history: two falls in the past three months, both occurring during gait freezing episodes at narrow spaces.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 24/30, losing points on delayed recall (3), verbal fluency (1), and trail-making (2). Speech is hypophonic with dysarthric quality but language content intact. Comprehension and repetition preserved. No aphasia or neglect.
neurological_exam.motor: Moderate cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist and left elbow; mild cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist. Marked bradykinesia in the left hand with prominent amplitude decrement and slowing on rapid alternating movements and finger tapping. Right hand bradykinesia is mild. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Resting tremor in the left hand, 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling character, intermittent and suppressible with purposeful movement. Subtle re-emergent tremor on left arm extension. No tremor observed in the right hand or lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact throughout. Vibration sense mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, age-appropriate.
